# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# surtgis_algorithms - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-algorithms/^0.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-algorithms)SurtGis Algorithms

Geospatial analysis algorithms for SurtGis.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-algorithm-categories)Available Algorithm Categories

- **terrain**: Slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, TPI, TRI, landform, TWI, SPI, STI, geomorphons, viewshed, SVF, openness, convergence, multiscale curvatures, feature-preserving smoothing, wind exposure, solar radiation, MRVBF/MRRTF, northness/eastness, DEV, multidirectional hillshade, shape index, curvedness, log transform, accumulation zones
- **hydrology**: Fill sinks, Priority-Flood, flow direction, flow accumulation, watershed, HAND, stream network
- **imagery**: Spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, NDRE, GNDVI, NGRDI, RECI, etc.), band math, reclassification
- **interpolation**: IDW, nearest neighbor, TIN
- **vector**: Buffer, simplify, spatial operations, clipping, measurements
- **morphology**: Erosion, dilation, opening, closing, gradient, top-hat, black-hat
- **statistics**: Focal statistics, zonal statistics, spatial autocorrelation

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# surtgis_colormap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-colormap/^0.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-colormap)SurtGis Colormap

Color mapping and raster-to-RGBA rendering for SurtGis.

Provides 8 predefined color schemes ported from the web demo, plus a generic
multi-stop interpolation engine. The main entry point is [ raster_to_rgba](https://docs.rs/fn.raster_to_rgba.html)
which converts a

`Raster<T>` into an RGBA pixel buffer suitable for GPU textures.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/struct.ColorStop.html)- Stop
- A color stop: position in [0, 1] mapped to an RGB color.
- [Colormap](https://docs.rs/struct.ColormapParams.html)- Params
- Parameters for colormap rendering.
- [Rgb](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html)
- RGB color as (r, g, b) with values in 0..=255.
- [Rgba](https://docs.rs/struct.RgbaImage.html)- Image
- Row-major 8-bit RGBA pixel buffer.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorScheme.html)- Scheme
- Available color schemes.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors produced when building or encoding an `RgbaImage`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_params.html)- params
- Auto-detect min/max from a raster, returning `ColormapParams`ready to use.
- [evaluate](https://docs.rs/fn.evaluate.html)
- Evaluate a color scheme at normalized position `t`∈ [0, 1].
- [raster_](https://docs.rs/fn.raster_to_rgba.html)- to_ - rgba
- Convert a raster to an RGBA pixel buffer.
- [rgba_](https://docs.rs/fn.rgba_to_png_bytes.html)- to_ - png_ - bytes
- Encode an arbitrary RGBA byte buffer as PNG. Native target only.
- [save_](https://docs.rs/fn.save_png.html)- png
- Write an RGBA buffer to `path`as a PNG. Native target only.

# surtgis_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-core/^0.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-core)SurtGis Core

Core types, traits and I/O for the SurtGis geospatial library.

This crate provides:

- `Raster<T>`: Generic raster grid type
- `GeoTransform`: Affine transformation for georeferencing
- `CRS`: Coordinate Reference System handling
- Algorithm traits for consistent API
- I/O for common geospatial formats
- Streaming (`StripProcessor``TileGrid`

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

As of v0.15.0, `surtgis-core` is the foundation of the SurtGIS
engine ecosystem and its public API is treated as **stable under
SemVer**: within a minor series the API only grows, and breaking
changes are pre-announced one release ahead in the CHANGELOG under
a `Breaking` heading. Sibling crates should depend on
`surtgis-core = "0.15"` alone; the CLI and GUI crates carry no
stability promise.

# surtgis_relief - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-relief/^0.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-relief)SurtGIS Relief

Rayshader-style shaded-relief compositing on top of the terrain primitives
that already live in `surtgis-algorithms`. This crate is a *compositor*,
not a new set of algorithms — see `SPEC_SURTGIS_RELIEF.md` in the
repository root for the full design.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-lives-here)What lives here

- `ray_shade`- `surtgis_algorithms::terrain::horizon_angle_map_fast`
- `sphere_shade`- `[0, 1]`, wrapping- `surtgis_algorithms::terrain::hillshade`

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-re-exported)What is re-exported

Pixel-buffer and PNG output live in
[ surtgis_colormap](https://docs.rs/surtgis-colormap/0.17.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/surtgis_colormap/index.html); we re-export the relevant types
at the crate root for ergonomics.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use surtgis_relief::{ray_shade, sphere_shade, RayShadeParams, SunSample, RgbaImage};
let shadow_mask = ray_shade(&dem, &RayShadeParams::default())?;
let mut img = RgbaImage::from_intensity(&sphere_shade(&dem, Default::default())?);
let shadow_layer = RgbaImage::from_intensity(&shadow_mask);
img.multiply(&shadow_layer, 0.5)?;
img.save_png("relief.png")?;
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Colormap](https://docs.rs/struct.ColormapParams.html)- Params
- Parameters for colormap rendering.
- [RayShade](https://docs.rs/struct.RayShadeParams.html)- Params
- Parameters for `ray_shade`
- [Relief](https://docs.rs/struct.ReliefBuilder.html)- Builder
- Order-preserving accumulator for relief layers.
- [Rgba](https://docs.rs/struct.RgbaImage.html)- Image
- Row-major 8-bit RGBA pixel buffer.
- [SunSample](https://docs.rs/struct.SunSample.html)
- A single sun position.
- [Water](https://docs.rs/struct.WaterParams.html)- Params
- Parameters for `detect_water`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorScheme.html)- Scheme
- Available color schemes.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors produced when building or encoding an `RgbaImage`
- [Relief](https://docs.rs/enum.ReliefError.html)- Error
- Errors produced by the relief crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [ambient_](https://docs.rs/fn.ambient_shade.html)- shade
- Compute the ambient-occlusion intensity layer.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_shadow_ray_mask.html)- shadow_ - ray_ - mask
- Per-cell binary shadow mask: `1.0`= lit,`0.0`= in shadow.
- [detect_](https://docs.rs/fn.detect_water.html)- water
- Detect water bodies as large flat connected components.
- [horizon_](https://docs.rs/fn.horizon_tan_map.html)- tan_ - map
- Per-cell maximum `tan(angle_to_occluder)`along a single azimuth.
- [ray_](https://docs.rs/fn.ray_shade.html)- shade
- Ray-traced cast shadows.
- [rgba_](https://docs.rs/fn.rgba_to_png_bytes.html)- to_ - png_ - bytes
- Encode an arbitrary RGBA byte buffer as PNG. Native target only.
- [save_](https://docs.rs/fn.save_png.html)- png
- Write an RGBA buffer to `path`as a PNG. Native target only.
- [sphere_](https://docs.rs/fn.sphere_shade.html)- shade
- Normal-based hillshade as intensity in `[0, 1]`.
- [water_](https://docs.rs/fn.water_depth.html)- depth
- Compute per-cell water depth from a binary water mask. Returns a
`Raster<f32>`where every water cell holds its 8-connected Chebyshev distance (in cells) to the nearest non-water neighbour. Shore cells → 1.0, deepest centres of large lakes → large values. Non-water cells return 0.0.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- `Result`alias scoped to this crate.

# wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/^0.2/

## Expand description

Runtime support for the `wasm-bindgen` tool

This crate contains the runtime support necessary for `wasm-bindgen` the
attribute and tool. Crates pull in the `#[wasm_bindgen]` attribute through
this crate and this crate also provides JS bindings through the `JsValue`
interface.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#enable-interning)`enable-interning`

Enables the internal cache for [`wasm_bindgen::intern`].

This feature currently enables the `std` feature, meaning that it is not
compatible with `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#std-default)`std` (default)

Enabling this feature will make the crate depend on the Rust standard library.

Disable this feature to use this crate in `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#strict-macro)`strict-macro`

All warnings the `#[wasm_bindgen]` macro emits are turned into hard errors.
This mainly affects unused attribute options.

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-features)Deprecated features

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-serialize)`serde-serialize`

**Deprecated:** Use the [ serde-wasm-bindgen](https://docs.rs/serde-wasm-bindgen/latest/serde_wasm_bindgen/) crate instead.

Enables the `JsValue::from_serde` and `JsValue::into_serde` methods for
serializing and deserializing Rust types to and from JavaScript.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)`spans`

**Deprecated:** This feature became a no-op in wasm-bindgen v0.2.20 (Sep 7, 2018).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::convert::`- [IntoJsGeneric](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html);
- `pub use crate::convert::`- [JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.JsGeneric.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [closure](https://docs.rs/closure/index.html)
- Support for closures in `wasm-bindgen`
- [convert](https://docs.rs/convert/index.html)
- ⚠️ Unstable
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- A module which is typically glob imported.
- [sys](https://docs.rs/sys/index.html)
- JavaScript system types that are re-exported by `js-sys`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [link_to](https://docs.rs/macro.link_to.html)
- This macro takes a JS module as input and returns a URL that can be used to access it at runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Clamped](https://docs.rs/struct.Clamped.html)
- A wrapper type around slices and vectors for binding the `Uint8ClampedArray`array in JS.
- [JsError](https://docs.rs/struct.JsError.html)
- Convenience type for use on exported `fn() -> Result<T, JsError>`functions, where you wish to throw a JavaScript`Error`object.
- [JsStatic](https://docs.rs/struct.JsStatic.html)- Deprecated
- Wrapper type for imported statics.
- [JsThread](https://docs.rs/struct.JsThreadLocal.html)- Local
- Wrapper type for imported statics.
- [JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)
- Representation of an object owned by JS.
- [Parent](https://docs.rs/struct.Parent.html)
- Storage wrapper for the auto-injected `parent`field on a struct that declares`#[wasm_bindgen(extends = Parent)]`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Erasable](https://docs.rs/trait.ErasableGeneric.html)- Generic
- Private marker trait for erasable generics - types with this trait have the same repr for all generic param values, and can therefore be transmuted on the singular Repr type representation on ABI boundaries.
- [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html)
- A trait for dynamic checked and unchecked casting between JS types.
- [Unwrap](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrapThrowExt.html)- Throw - Ext
- An extension trait for `Option<T>`and`Result<T, E>`for unwrapping the`T`value, or throwing a JS error if it is not available.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [exports](https://docs.rs/fn.exports.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Instance.prototype.exports`
- [externref_](https://docs.rs/fn.externref_heap_live_count.html)- heap_ - live_ - count
- Get the count of live `externref`s /`JsValue`s in`wasm-bindgen`’s heap.
- [function_](https://docs.rs/fn.function_table.html)- table
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Table`which is the indirect function table used by Rust
- [instance](https://docs.rs/fn.instance.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Instance`. This is only available when the final Wasm app is built with`--target no-modules`,`--target web`,`--target deno`or`--target nodejs`. It is unavailable for`--target bundler`.
- [intern](https://docs.rs/fn.intern.html)
- Interns Rust strings so that it’s much faster to send them to JS.
- [memory](https://docs.rs/fn.memory.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Memory`
- [module](https://docs.rs/fn.module.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Module`. This is only available when the final Wasm app is built with`--target no-modules`,`--target web`,`--target deno`or`--target nodejs`. It is unavailable for`--target bundler`.
- [throw_](https://docs.rs/fn.throw_str.html)- str
- Throws a JS exception.
- [throw_](https://docs.rs/fn.throw_val.html)- val
- Rethrow a JS exception

# surtgis_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/surtgis-wasm/0.17.0/target-redirect/surtgis_wasm/

## Expand description

WebAssembly bindings for SurtGis geospatial algorithms.

Exposes terrain, hydrology, imagery, interpolation, morphology, and
statistics functions to JavaScript. Input/output is via in-memory
GeoTIFF byte buffers (`&[u8]` / `Vec<u8>`).

No competitor offers terrain analysis + hydrology in WASM.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [advanced_](https://docs.rs/fn.advanced_curvature.html)- curvature
- Compute one of Florinsky’s 14 curvatures from a DEM. `ctype`accepts:`mean_h`,`gaussian_k`,`unsphericity_m`,`difference_e`,`kmin`,`kmax`,`kh`(horizontal),`kv`(vertical),`khe`(horizontal excess),`kve`(vertical excess),`ka`(accumulation),`kr`(ring),`rotor`,`laplacian`.
- [aspect_](https://docs.rs/fn.aspect_degrees.html)- degrees
- Compute aspect in degrees (0-360, 0=North, clockwise).
- [bsi](https://docs.rs/fn.bsi.html)
- BSI (Bare Soil Index) from SWIR, Red, NIR, and Blue bands.
- [curvature_](https://docs.rs/fn.curvature_compute.html)- compute
- Compute curvature. `ctype`: “general”, “profile”, “plan”.
- [curvedness](https://docs.rs/fn.curvedness.html)
- Compute curvedness.
- [dev_](https://docs.rs/fn.dev_compute.html)- compute
- Compute DEV (Deviation from Mean Elevation). `radius`: window radius.
- [eastness_](https://docs.rs/fn.eastness_compute.html)- compute
- Compute eastness (sin of aspect).
- [evi](https://docs.rs/fn.evi.html)
- EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index) from NIR, Red, and Blue bands. Uses default EVI coefficients (G=2.5, L=1, C1=6, C2=7.5).
- [evi2](https://docs.rs/fn.evi2.html)
- EVI2 (Enhanced Vegetation Index, 2-band variant) from NIR and Red bands.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_depressions.html)- depressions
- Fill sinks (depressions) in a DEM.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_d8.html)- accumulation_ - d8
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_dinf_compute.html)- accumulation_ - dinf_ - compute
- Compute D-infinity flow accumulation (contributing area in cell counts).
Internally computes the directions and the accumulation in one pass; if
you need the angles separately, use `flow_direction_dinf_compute`first.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_mfd_compute.html)- accumulation_ - mfd_ - compute
- Compute flow accumulation from a D8 flow direction raster. Compute MFD (Multiple Flow Direction) accumulation directly from a DEM. Distributes flow proportionally to all downslope neighbors based on slope, better representing sheet flow on gentle terrain than D8.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_direction_d8.html)- direction_ - d8
- Compute D8 flow direction from a filled DEM. Returns encoded direction raster.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_direction_dinf_compute.html)- direction_ - dinf_ - compute
- Compute D-infinity flow direction angles (radians, 0 = East, CCW). NaN for nodata/pit cells. Reference implementation matches TauDEM.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_majority.html)- majority
- Focal majority (mode). Useful for categorical rasters.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_max.html)- max
- Focal maximum.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_mean.html)- mean
- Focal mean statistic. `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_median.html)- median
- Focal median.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_min.html)- min
- Focal minimum.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_percentile.html)- percentile
- Focal percentile. `percentile`in [0, 100]; e.g. 50 = median, 25 = Q1.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_range.html)- range
- Focal range (max - min). `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_std.html)- std
- Focal standard deviation. `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_sum.html)- sum
- Focal sum.
- [geomorphons_](https://docs.rs/fn.geomorphons_compute.html)- compute
- Compute geomorphons landform classification.
`flatness`: flatness threshold degrees.`radius`: search radius in cells.
- [gndvi](https://docs.rs/fn.gndvi.html)
- GNDVI (Green NDVI) from NIR and Green bands.
- [hand_](https://docs.rs/fn.hand_compute.html)- compute
- Compute HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) from a DEM.
Internally computes fill → flow_direction → flow_accumulation → HAND.
`stream_threshold`: accumulation threshold to define streams (default 1000).
- [hillshade_](https://docs.rs/fn.hillshade_compute.html)- compute
- Compute hillshade. `azimuth`: sun azimuth (default 315).`altitude`: sun altitude (default 45).
- [mndwi](https://docs.rs/fn.mndwi.html)
- MNDWI (Modified NDWI) from Green and SWIR bands.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_closing.html)- closing
- Morphological closing (dilation followed by erosion).
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_dilate.html)- dilate
- Morphological dilation with square kernel of given `radius`.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_erode.html)- erode
- Morphological erosion with square kernel of given `radius`.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_opening.html)- opening
- Morphological opening (erosion followed by dilation).
- [mrvbf](https://docs.rs/fn.mrvbf.html)
- MRVBF — Multi-Resolution Valley Bottom Flatness (Gallant & Dowling 2003). Returns only the MRVBF raster (companion MRRTF dropped); if you need both, expose via the native Rust API.
- [msavi](https://docs.rs/fn.msavi.html)
- MSAVI (Modified SAVI) from NIR and Red bands. Auto-adjusts L factor.
- [multidirectional_](https://docs.rs/fn.multidirectional_hillshade.html)- hillshade
- Compute multidirectional hillshade (6 azimuths combined).
- [nbr](https://docs.rs/fn.nbr.html)
- NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio) from NIR and SWIR bands.
- [ndbi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndbi.html)
- NDBI (Normalized Difference Built-up Index) from SWIR and NIR bands.
- [ndmi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndmi.html)
- NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index) from NIR and SWIR bands.
- [ndre](https://docs.rs/fn.ndre.html)
- NDRE (Normalized Difference Red Edge) from NIR and Red Edge bands.
- [ndvi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndvi.html)
- Compute NDVI from NIR and Red bands.
- [ndwi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndwi.html)
- Compute NDWI (Normalized Difference Water Index) from Green and NIR bands.
- [normalized_](https://docs.rs/fn.normalized_diff.html)- diff
- Compute generic Normalized Difference Index: (A - B) / (A + B).
- [northness_](https://docs.rs/fn.northness_compute.html)- compute
- Compute northness (cos of aspect).
- [openness_](https://docs.rs/fn.openness_negative.html)- negative
- Negative openness — visibility of the ground below each cell. High values = concave hollows / valleys.
- [openness_](https://docs.rs/fn.openness_positive.html)- positive
- Positive openness — visibility of the sky above each cell across `n_dirs`directions out to`radius`cells. High values = exposed ridges/peaks.
- [priority_](https://docs.rs/fn.priority_flood_fill.html)- flood_ - fill
- Priority-flood depression filling (Barnes 2014).
- [relief_](https://docs.rs/fn.relief_compute.html)- compute
- Full shaded-relief composite. Returns a raw RGBA `Vec<u8>`of length`width * height * 4`in row-major order; the caller knows`width × height`from the DEM and can either encode a PNG on the JS side or upload it directly as a canvas/WebGL texture.
- [savi](https://docs.rs/fn.savi.html)
- Compute SAVI (Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index). `l_factor`: soil adjustment (default 0.5).
- [shape_](https://docs.rs/fn.shape_index.html)- index
- Compute shape index.
- [sky_](https://docs.rs/fn.sky_view_factor.html)- view_ - factor
- Compute sky view factor. `n_dirs`: number of directions.`max_radius`: search radius in cells.
- [slope](https://docs.rs/fn.slope.html)
- Compute slope from a DEM. `units`: “degrees” (default) or “percent”.
- [ssa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ssa_2d_denoise.html)- 2d_ - denoise
- Denoise DEM using 2D-SSA. `window`: window size,`components`: number of signal components.
- [tpi_](https://docs.rs/fn.tpi_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TPI (Topographic Position Index). `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [tri_](https://docs.rs/fn.tri_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TRI (Terrain Ruggedness Index).
- [twi_](https://docs.rs/fn.twi_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TWI (Topographic Wetness Index) from a DEM. Internally computes fill → flow_direction → flow_accumulation → slope → TWI.
- [uncertainty_](https://docs.rs/fn.uncertainty_slope.html)- slope
- Compute slope uncertainty (RMSE). `dem_rmse`: DEM vertical RMSE in meters.

# surtgis_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-wasm/0.17.0/surtgis_wasm/index.html

## Expand description

WebAssembly bindings for SurtGis geospatial algorithms.

Exposes terrain, hydrology, imagery, interpolation, morphology, and
statistics functions to JavaScript. Input/output is via in-memory
GeoTIFF byte buffers (`&[u8]` / `Vec<u8>`).

No competitor offers terrain analysis + hydrology in WASM.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [advanced_](https://docs.rs/fn.advanced_curvature.html)- curvature
- Compute one of Florinsky’s 14 curvatures from a DEM. `ctype`accepts:`mean_h`,`gaussian_k`,`unsphericity_m`,`difference_e`,`kmin`,`kmax`,`kh`(horizontal),`kv`(vertical),`khe`(horizontal excess),`kve`(vertical excess),`ka`(accumulation),`kr`(ring),`rotor`,`laplacian`.
- [aspect_](https://docs.rs/fn.aspect_degrees.html)- degrees
- Compute aspect in degrees (0-360, 0=North, clockwise).
- [bsi](https://docs.rs/fn.bsi.html)
- BSI (Bare Soil Index) from SWIR, Red, NIR, and Blue bands.
- [curvature_](https://docs.rs/fn.curvature_compute.html)- compute
- Compute curvature. `ctype`: “general”, “profile”, “plan”.
- [curvedness](https://docs.rs/fn.curvedness.html)
- Compute curvedness.
- [dev_](https://docs.rs/fn.dev_compute.html)- compute
- Compute DEV (Deviation from Mean Elevation). `radius`: window radius.
- [eastness_](https://docs.rs/fn.eastness_compute.html)- compute
- Compute eastness (sin of aspect).
- [evi](https://docs.rs/fn.evi.html)
- EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index) from NIR, Red, and Blue bands. Uses default EVI coefficients (G=2.5, L=1, C1=6, C2=7.5).
- [evi2](https://docs.rs/fn.evi2.html)
- EVI2 (Enhanced Vegetation Index, 2-band variant) from NIR and Red bands.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_depressions.html)- depressions
- Fill sinks (depressions) in a DEM.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_d8.html)- accumulation_ - d8
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_dinf_compute.html)- accumulation_ - dinf_ - compute
- Compute D-infinity flow accumulation (contributing area in cell counts).
Internally computes the directions and the accumulation in one pass; if
you need the angles separately, use `flow_direction_dinf_compute`first.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_accumulation_mfd_compute.html)- accumulation_ - mfd_ - compute
- Compute flow accumulation from a D8 flow direction raster. Compute MFD (Multiple Flow Direction) accumulation directly from a DEM. Distributes flow proportionally to all downslope neighbors based on slope, better representing sheet flow on gentle terrain than D8.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_direction_d8.html)- direction_ - d8
- Compute D8 flow direction from a filled DEM. Returns encoded direction raster.
- [flow_](https://docs.rs/fn.flow_direction_dinf_compute.html)- direction_ - dinf_ - compute
- Compute D-infinity flow direction angles (radians, 0 = East, CCW). NaN for nodata/pit cells. Reference implementation matches TauDEM.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_majority.html)- majority
- Focal majority (mode). Useful for categorical rasters.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_max.html)- max
- Focal maximum.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_mean.html)- mean
- Focal mean statistic. `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_median.html)- median
- Focal median.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_min.html)- min
- Focal minimum.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_percentile.html)- percentile
- Focal percentile. `percentile`in [0, 100]; e.g. 50 = median, 25 = Q1.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_range.html)- range
- Focal range (max - min). `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_std.html)- std
- Focal standard deviation. `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [focal_](https://docs.rs/fn.focal_sum.html)- sum
- Focal sum.
- [geomorphons_](https://docs.rs/fn.geomorphons_compute.html)- compute
- Compute geomorphons landform classification.
`flatness`: flatness threshold degrees.`radius`: search radius in cells.
- [gndvi](https://docs.rs/fn.gndvi.html)
- GNDVI (Green NDVI) from NIR and Green bands.
- [hand_](https://docs.rs/fn.hand_compute.html)- compute
- Compute HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) from a DEM.
Internally computes fill → flow_direction → flow_accumulation → HAND.
`stream_threshold`: accumulation threshold to define streams (default 1000).
- [hillshade_](https://docs.rs/fn.hillshade_compute.html)- compute
- Compute hillshade. `azimuth`: sun azimuth (default 315).`altitude`: sun altitude (default 45).
- [mndwi](https://docs.rs/fn.mndwi.html)
- MNDWI (Modified NDWI) from Green and SWIR bands.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_closing.html)- closing
- Morphological closing (dilation followed by erosion).
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_dilate.html)- dilate
- Morphological dilation with square kernel of given `radius`.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_erode.html)- erode
- Morphological erosion with square kernel of given `radius`.
- [morph_](https://docs.rs/fn.morph_opening.html)- opening
- Morphological opening (erosion followed by dilation).
- [mrvbf](https://docs.rs/fn.mrvbf.html)
- MRVBF — Multi-Resolution Valley Bottom Flatness (Gallant & Dowling 2003). Returns only the MRVBF raster (companion MRRTF dropped); if you need both, expose via the native Rust API.
- [msavi](https://docs.rs/fn.msavi.html)
- MSAVI (Modified SAVI) from NIR and Red bands. Auto-adjusts L factor.
- [multidirectional_](https://docs.rs/fn.multidirectional_hillshade.html)- hillshade
- Compute multidirectional hillshade (6 azimuths combined).
- [nbr](https://docs.rs/fn.nbr.html)
- NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio) from NIR and SWIR bands.
- [ndbi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndbi.html)
- NDBI (Normalized Difference Built-up Index) from SWIR and NIR bands.
- [ndmi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndmi.html)
- NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index) from NIR and SWIR bands.
- [ndre](https://docs.rs/fn.ndre.html)
- NDRE (Normalized Difference Red Edge) from NIR and Red Edge bands.
- [ndvi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndvi.html)
- Compute NDVI from NIR and Red bands.
- [ndwi](https://docs.rs/fn.ndwi.html)
- Compute NDWI (Normalized Difference Water Index) from Green and NIR bands.
- [normalized_](https://docs.rs/fn.normalized_diff.html)- diff
- Compute generic Normalized Difference Index: (A - B) / (A + B).
- [northness_](https://docs.rs/fn.northness_compute.html)- compute
- Compute northness (cos of aspect).
- [openness_](https://docs.rs/fn.openness_negative.html)- negative
- Negative openness — visibility of the ground below each cell. High values = concave hollows / valleys.
- [openness_](https://docs.rs/fn.openness_positive.html)- positive
- Positive openness — visibility of the sky above each cell across `n_dirs`directions out to`radius`cells. High values = exposed ridges/peaks.
- [priority_](https://docs.rs/fn.priority_flood_fill.html)- flood_ - fill
- Priority-flood depression filling (Barnes 2014).
- [relief_](https://docs.rs/fn.relief_compute.html)- compute
- Full shaded-relief composite. Returns a raw RGBA `Vec<u8>`of length`width * height * 4`in row-major order; the caller knows`width × height`from the DEM and can either encode a PNG on the JS side or upload it directly as a canvas/WebGL texture.
- [savi](https://docs.rs/fn.savi.html)
- Compute SAVI (Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index). `l_factor`: soil adjustment (default 0.5).
- [shape_](https://docs.rs/fn.shape_index.html)- index
- Compute shape index.
- [sky_](https://docs.rs/fn.sky_view_factor.html)- view_ - factor
- Compute sky view factor. `n_dirs`: number of directions.`max_radius`: search radius in cells.
- [slope](https://docs.rs/fn.slope.html)
- Compute slope from a DEM. `units`: “degrees” (default) or “percent”.
- [ssa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ssa_2d_denoise.html)- 2d_ - denoise
- Denoise DEM using 2D-SSA. `window`: window size,`components`: number of signal components.
- [tpi_](https://docs.rs/fn.tpi_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TPI (Topographic Position Index). `radius`: window radius in cells.
- [tri_](https://docs.rs/fn.tri_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TRI (Terrain Ruggedness Index).
- [twi_](https://docs.rs/fn.twi_compute.html)- compute
- Compute TWI (Topographic Wetness Index) from a DEM. Internally computes fill → flow_direction → flow_accumulation → slope → TWI.
- [uncertainty_](https://docs.rs/fn.uncertainty_slope.html)- slope
- Compute slope uncertainty (RMSE). `dem_rmse`: DEM vertical RMSE in meters.

[41](#41)macro_rules! dem_op {
[43](#43)    ($tiff:expr, $body:expr) => {{
[44](#44)        let dem = read_geotiff_from_buffer::<f64>($tiff, None)
[45](#45)            .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[46](#46)        let result = ($body)(&dem).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[47](#47)        write_geotiff_to_buffer(&result, None).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))
[48](#48)    }};
[49](#49)}

[66](#66)            z_factor: 1.0
[67](#67)        }
[68](#68)    ))

[106](#106)pub fn curvature_compute(tiff_bytes: &[u8], ctype: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {

[108](#108)        "profile" => CurvatureType::Profile,

[110](#110)        _ => CurvatureType::General,

[122](#122)#[wasm_bindgen]
[132](#132)pub fn advanced_curvature(tiff_bytes: &[u8], ctype: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
[133](#133)    let ct = match ctype.to_lowercase().as_str() {
[134](#134)        "mean_h" | "mean" | "h" => AdvancedCurvatureType::MeanH,
[135](#135)        "gaussian_k" | "gaussian" | "k" => AdvancedCurvatureType::GaussianK,
[136](#136)        "unsphericity_m" | "unsphericity" | "m" => AdvancedCurvatureType::UnsphericitytM,
[137](#137)        "difference_e" | "difference" | "e" => AdvancedCurvatureType::DifferenceE,
[138](#138)        "kmin" | "minimal" => AdvancedCurvatureType::MinimalKmin,
[139](#139)        "kmax" | "maximal" => AdvancedCurvatureType::MaximalKmax,
[140](#140)        "kh" | "horizontal" => AdvancedCurvatureType::HorizontalKh,
[141](#141)        "kv" | "vertical" => AdvancedCurvatureType::VerticalKv,
[142](#142)        "khe" | "horizontal_excess" => AdvancedCurvatureType::HorizontalExcessKhe,
[143](#143)        "kve" | "vertical_excess" => AdvancedCurvatureType::VerticalExcessKve,
[144](#144)        "ka" | "accumulation" => AdvancedCurvatureType::AccumulationKa,
[145](#145)        "kr" | "ring" => AdvancedCurvatureType::RingKr,
[146](#146)        "rotor" => AdvancedCurvatureType::Rotor,
[147](#147)        "laplacian" => AdvancedCurvatureType::Laplacian,
[148](#148)        other => {
[149](#149)            return Err(JsValue::from_str(&format!(
[150](#150)                "unknown advanced curvature type: '{}'. Valid: mean_h, gaussian_k, unsphericity_m, difference_e, kmin, kmax, kh, kv, khe, kve, ka, kr, rotor, laplacian",
[151](#151)                other
[152](#152)            )));
[153](#153)        }
[154](#154)    };
[155](#155)    dem_op!(tiff_bytes, |dem: &_| advanced_curvatures(dem, ct))
[156](#156)}

[169](#169)
[170](#170)#[wasm_bindgen]
[173](#173)pub fn twi_compute(tiff_bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
[174](#174)    let dem = read_geotiff_from_buffer::<f64>(tiff_bytes, None)
[175](#175)        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[176](#176)    let filled = fill_sinks(&dem, FillSinksParams::default())
[177](#177)        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[178](#178)    let fdir = flow_direction(&filled).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[179](#179)    let facc = flow_accumulation(&fdir).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[180](#180)    let slp = compute_slope(
[181](#181)        &dem,
[182](#182)        SlopeParams {
[183](#183)            units: SlopeUnits::Degrees,
[184](#184)            z_factor: 1.0,
[185](#185)        },
[186](#186)    )
[187](#187)    .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[188](#188)    let result = compute_twi(&facc, &slp).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[189](#189)    write_geotiff_to_buffer(&result, None).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))
[190](#190)}

[463](#463)macro_rules! two_band_index {
[465](#465)    ($a:expr, $b:expr, $f:expr) => {{
[466](#466)        let a = read_geotiff_from_buffer::<f64>($a, None)
[467](#467)            .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[468](#468)        let b = read_geotiff_from_buffer::<f64>($b, None)
[469](#469)            .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[470](#470)        let result = ($f)(&a, &b).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[471](#471)        write_geotiff_to_buffer(&result, None).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))
[472](#472)    }};
[473](#473)}

[716](#716)#[wasm_bindgen]
[734](#734)pub fn relief_compute(
[735](#735)    tiff_bytes: &[u8],
[736](#736)    colormap: &str,
[737](#737)    sun_azimuth: f64,
[738](#738)    sun_altitude: f64,
[739](#739)    shadows: bool,
[740](#740)    ambient: bool,
[741](#741)) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
[742](#742)    use surtgis_colormap::ColorScheme;
[743](#743)    use surtgis_relief::{RayShadeParams, ReliefBuilder, ambient_shade, ray_shade, sphere_shade};
[744](#744)
[745](#745)    let scheme = match colormap.to_ascii_lowercase().as_str() {
[746](#746)        "divergent" => ColorScheme::Divergent,
[747](#747)        "grayscale" | "greyscale" => ColorScheme::Grayscale,
[748](#748)        "ndvi" => ColorScheme::Ndvi,
[749](#749)        "bwr" | "blue-white-red" => ColorScheme::BlueWhiteRed,
[750](#750)        "geomorphons" => ColorScheme::Geomorphons,
[751](#751)        "water" => ColorScheme::Water,
[752](#752)        "accumulation" => ColorScheme::Accumulation,
[753](#753)        _ => ColorScheme::Terrain,
[754](#754)    };
[755](#755)
[756](#756)    let dem = read_geotiff_from_buffer::<f64>(tiff_bytes, None)
[757](#757)        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[758](#758)
[759](#759)    let sphere = sphere_shade(
[760](#760)        &dem,
[761](#761)        HillshadeParams {
[762](#762)            azimuth: sun_azimuth,
[763](#763)            altitude: sun_altitude,
[764](#764)            z_factor: 1.0,
[765](#765)            normalized: true,
[766](#766)        },
[767](#767)    )
[768](#768)    .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[769](#769)
[770](#770)    let mut builder = ReliefBuilder::new(&dem)
[771](#771)        .base_colormap(scheme)
[772](#772)        .add_shade(sphere, 0.6);
[773](#773)
[774](#774)    if shadows {
[775](#775)        let (rows, cols) = dem.shape();
[776](#776)        let params = RayShadeParams::with_soft_shadow_altitude(
[777](#777)            sun_azimuth,
[778](#778)            (sun_altitude - 5.0).max(0.5),
[779](#779)            (sun_altitude + 5.0).min(89.0),
[780](#780)            11,
[781](#781)        );
[782](#782)        let params = RayShadeParams {
[783](#783)            suns: params.suns,
[784](#784)            radius: rows.max(cols),
[785](#785)        };
[786](#786)        let shadow = ray_shade(&dem, ¶ms).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[787](#787)        builder = builder.add_shadow(shadow, 0.7);
[788](#788)    }
[789](#789)
[790](#790)    if ambient {
[791](#791)        let ao = ambient_shade(&dem, 30).map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[792](#792)        builder = builder.add_ambient(ao, 0.3);
[793](#793)    }
[794](#794)
[795](#795)    let img = builder
[796](#796)        .render()
[797](#797)        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
[798](#798)    Ok(img.pixels)
[799](#799)}

---

# advanced_curvature in surtgis_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-wasm/0.17.0/surtgis_wasm/fn.advanced_curvature.html

## Expand description

Compute one of Florinsky’s 14 curvatures from a DEM. `ctype` accepts:
`mean_h`, `gaussian_k`, `unsphericity_m`, `difference_e`, `kmin`, `kmax`,
`kh` (horizontal), `kv` (vertical), `khe` (horizontal excess), `kve`
(vertical excess), `ka` (accumulation), `kr` (ring), `rotor`, `laplacian`.

SurtGIS is the only library that exposes the complete 14-curvature system from a single binary, and the only one that does it in the browser via WebAssembly. See paper §2.3.2 for definitions and references.

---

## Expand description

# flow_accumulation_mfd_compute in surtgis_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-wasm/0.17.0/surtgis_wasm/fn.flow_accumulation_mfd_compute.html

## Expand description

Compute flow accumulation from a D8 flow direction raster. Compute MFD (Multiple Flow Direction) accumulation directly from a DEM. Distributes flow proportionally to all downslope neighbors based on slope, better representing sheet flow on gentle terrain than D8.

# relief_compute in surtgis_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-wasm/0.17.0/surtgis_wasm/fn.relief_compute.html

```
pub fn relief_compute(
    tiff_bytes: &[
```
[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    colormap: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    sun_azimuth: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html),
    sun_altitude: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html),
    shadows: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
    ambient: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>, [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.114/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)>## Expand description

Full shaded-relief composite. Returns a raw RGBA `Vec<u8>` of length
`width * height * 4` in row-major order; the caller knows
`width × height` from the DEM and can either encode a PNG on the JS
side or upload it directly as a canvas/WebGL texture.

`colormap`: scheme name (`"terrain"`, `"grayscale"`, `"divergent"`,
`"ndvi"`, `"bwr"`, `"geomorphons"`, `"water"`, `"accumulation"`).
Unknown names fall back to `"terrain"`.

`shadows`: if true, runs `ray_shade` with 11 sun samples sharing the
azimuth (rayshader anglebreaks recipe — hits the amortised path).

`ambient`: if true, runs `ambient_shade` (SVF) with radius=30.

---

# byteorder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/byteorder/^1.4.3/

## Expand description

This crate provides convenience methods for encoding and decoding numbers in
either [big-endian or little-endian order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endianness).

The organization of the crate is pretty simple. A trait, [ ByteOrder](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteOrder.html), specifies
byte conversion methods for each type of number in Rust (sans numbers that have
a platform dependent size like

`usize` and `isize`). Two types, [and](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)

`BigEndian`[implement these methods. Finally,](https://docs.rs/enum.LittleEndian.html)

`LittleEndian`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.ReadBytesExt.html)

`ReadBytesExt`[provide convenience methods available to all types that implement](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteBytesExt.html)

`WriteBytesExt`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`Read`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`Write`An alias, [ NetworkEndian](https://docs.rs/type.NetworkEndian.html), for

[is provided to help improve code clarity.](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)

`BigEndian`An additional alias, [ NativeEndian](https://docs.rs/type.NativeEndian.html), is provided for the endianness of the
local platform. This is convenient when serializing data for use and
conversions are not desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Read unsigned 16 bit big-endian integers from a [ Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html) type:

```
use std::io::Cursor;
use byteorder::{BigEndian, ReadBytesExt};
let mut rdr = Cursor::new(vec![2, 5, 3, 0]);
// Note that we use type parameters to indicate which kind of byte order
// we want!
assert_eq!(517, rdr.read_u16::<BigEndian>().unwrap());
assert_eq!(768, rdr.read_u16::<BigEndian>().unwrap());
```
Write unsigned 16 bit little-endian integers to a [ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) type:

```
use byteorder::{LittleEndian, WriteBytesExt};
let mut wtr = vec![];
wtr.write_u16::<LittleEndian>(517).unwrap();
wtr.write_u16::<LittleEndian>(768).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wtr, vec![5, 2, 0, 3]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

This crate optionally provides support for 128 bit values (`i128` and `u128`)
when built with the `i128` feature enabled.

This crate can also be used without the standard library.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternatives)Alternatives

Note that as of Rust 1.32, the standard numeric types provide built-in methods
like `to_le_bytes` and `from_le_bytes`, which support some of the same use
cases.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [BigEndian](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)
- Defines big-endian serialization.
- [Little](https://docs.rs/enum.LittleEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines little-endian serialization.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteOrder.html)- Order
- `ByteOrder`describes types that can serialize integers as bytes.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/trait.ReadBytesExt.html)- Bytes - Ext
- Extends `Read``std::io`.)
- [Write](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteBytesExt.html)- Bytes - Ext
- Extends `Write``std::io`.)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BE](https://docs.rs/type.BE.html)
- A type alias for `BigEndian`
- [LE](https://docs.rs/type.LE.html)
- A type alias for `LittleEndian`
- [Native](https://docs.rs/type.NativeEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines system native-endian serialization.
- [Network](https://docs.rs/type.NetworkEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines network byte order serialization.

# cudarc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cudarc/^0.19.4/

## Expand description

Safe CUDA wrappers for:

| library | dynamic load | dynamic link | static link |
|---|---|---|---|
| [CUDA driver](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/index.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| [NVRTC](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvrtc/index.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuRAND](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/curand/index.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuBLAS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuBLASLt](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/#using-the-cublaslt-api) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [NCCL](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuDNN](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/cudnn/backend/latest/api/overview.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuSPARSE](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cusparse/) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [cuSOLVER](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cusolver/) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| [cuFILE](https://docs.nvidia.com/gpudirect-storage/api-reference-guide/index.html#introduction) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [CUPTI](https://docs.nvidia.com/cupti/) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| [nvtx](https://nvidia.github.io/NVTX/) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| [cuTENSOR](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cutensor/index.html) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |

CUDA Versions supported

- 11.4-11.8
- 12.0-12.9
- 13.0

CUDNN versions supported:

- 9.12.0

NCCL versions supported:

- 2.28.3

[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-cuda-version)Configuring CUDA version

Select cuda version with one of:

- `-F cuda-version-from-build-system`: At build time will get the cuda toolkit version using- `nvcc`- `-F fallback-latest`: can be used to control behavior if this fails. default is not enabled, which will cause the build script to panic. if- `-F fallback-latest`is enabled, we will use the highest bindings we have.

- `-F cuda-<major>0<minor>0`to build for a specific version of cuda

[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-linking)Configuring linking

By default we use `-F dynamic-loading`, which will not require any libraries to be present at build time.

You can also enable `-F dynamic-linking` or `-F static-linking` for your use case.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

**See  driver for more examples**

At the core is the [driver](https://docs.rs/driver/index.html) API, which exposes a bunch of structs, but the main ones are:

- `driver::CudaContext`
- `driver::CudaStream`
- `driver::CudaSlice<T>`- `Vec<T>`- `driver::CudaStream`

Here is a table of similar concepts between CPU and Cuda:

| Concept | CPU | Cuda |
|---|---|---|
| Memory allocator | `std::alloc::GlobalAlloc` | `driver::CudaContext` |
| List of values on heap | `Vec<T>` | `driver::CudaSlice<T>` |
| Slice | `&[T]` | `driver::CudaView<T>` |
| Mutable Slice | `&mut [T]` | `driver::CudaViewMut<T>` |
| Function | `Fn` | `driver::CudaFunction` |
| Calling a function | `my_function(a, b, c)` | `driver::LaunchArgs::launch()` |
| Thread | `std::thread::Thread` | `driver::CudaStream` |

[§](https://docs.rs#combining-the-different-apis)Combining the different APIs

All the highest level apis have been designed to work together.

[§](https://docs.rs#nvrtc)nvrtc

[ nvrtc::compile_ptx()](https://docs.rs/nvrtc/safe/fn.compile_ptx.html) outputs a

[, which can be loaded into a device with](https://docs.rs/nvrtc/safe/struct.Ptx.html)

`nvrtc::Ptx`[.](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/struct.CudaContext.html#method.load_module)

`driver::CudaContext::load_module()`[§](https://docs.rs#cublas)cublas

[cublas::CudaBlas](https://docs.rs/cublas/safe/struct.CudaBlas.html) can perform gemm operations using [ cublas::Gemm<T>](https://docs.rs/cublas/safe/trait.Gemm.html),
and

[. Both of these traits can generically accept memory allocated by the driver in the form of:](https://docs.rs/cublas/safe/trait.Gemv.html)

`cublas::Gemv<T>`[,](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/struct.CudaSlice.html)

`driver::CudaSlice<T>`[, and](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/struct.CudaView.html)

`driver::CudaView<T>`[.](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/struct.CudaViewMut.html)

`driver::CudaViewMut<T>`[§](https://docs.rs#curand)curand

[curand::CudaRng](https://docs.rs/curand/safe/struct.CudaRng.html) can fill a [ driver::CudaSlice<T>](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/struct.CudaSlice.html) with random data, based on
one of its available distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#combining-saferesultsys)Combining safe/result/sys

The result and sys levels are very inter-changeable for each API. However, the safe apis don’t necessarily allow you to mix in the result level. This is to encourage going through the safe API when possible.

**If you need some functionality that isn’t present in the safe api, please
open a ticket.**

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-organization)crate organization

Each of the modules for the above is organized into three levels:

- A `safe`module which provides safe abstractions over the`result`module
- A `result`which is a thin wrapper around the`sys`module to ensure all functions return[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)
- A `sys`module which contains the raw FFI bindings

| API | Safe | Result | Sys |
|---|---|---|---|
| driver | [driver::safe](https://docs.rs/driver/safe/index.html) | [driver::result](https://docs.rs/driver/result/index.html) | [driver::sys](https://docs.rs/driver/sys/index.html) |
| cublas | [cublas::safe](https://docs.rs/cublas/safe/index.html) | [cublas::result](https://docs.rs/cublas/result/index.html) | [cublas::sys](https://docs.rs/cublas/sys/index.html) |
| cublaslt | [cublaslt::safe](https://docs.rs/cublaslt/safe/index.html) | [cublaslt::result](https://docs.rs/cublaslt/result/index.html) | [cublaslt::sys](https://docs.rs/cublaslt/sys/index.html) |
| nvrtc | [nvrtc::safe](https://docs.rs/nvrtc/safe/index.html) | [nvrtc::result](https://docs.rs/nvrtc/result/index.html) | [nvrtc::sys](https://docs.rs/nvrtc/sys/index.html) |
| curand | [curand::safe](https://docs.rs/curand/safe/index.html) | [curand::result](https://docs.rs/curand/result/index.html) | [curand::sys](https://docs.rs/curand/sys/index.html) |
| cudnn | [cudnn::safe](https://docs.rs/cudnn/safe/index.html) | [cudnn::result](https://docs.rs/cudnn/result/index.html) | [cudnn::sys](https://docs.rs/cudnn/sys/index.html) |
| cufft | [cufft::safe](https://docs.rs/cufft/safe/index.html) | [cufft::result](https://docs.rs/cufft/result/index.html) | [cufft::sys](https://docs.rs/cufft/sys/index.html) |
| cusparse | - | [cusparse::result](https://docs.rs/cusparse/result/index.html) | [cusparse::sys](https://docs.rs/cusparse/sys/index.html) |
| cusolver | [cusolver::safe](https://docs.rs/cusolver/safe/index.html) | [cusolver::result](https://docs.rs/cusolver/result/index.html) | [cusolver::sys](https://docs.rs/cusolver/sys/index.html) |
| cusolvermg | [cusolvermg::safe](https://docs.rs/cusolvermg/safe/index.html) | [cusolvermg::result](https://docs.rs/cusolvermg/result/index.html) | [cusolvermg::sys](https://docs.rs/cusolvermg/sys/index.html) |

| cutensor | [cutensor::safe] | [cutensor::result](https://docs.rs/cutensor/result/index.html) | [cutensor::sys](https://docs.rs/cutensor/sys/index.html) |

# float8 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/float8/^0.7.0/

## Expand description

Eight bit floating point types in Rust.

This crate provides 2 types:

- `F8E4M3`
- `F8E5M2`- `f16`

Generally, this crate is modelled after the [ half](https://docs.rs/half/2.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html) crate, so it can be
used alongside and with minimal code changes.

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

When the `serde` feature is enabled, [ F8E4M3](https://docs.rs/struct.F8E4M3.html) and

[will be serialized as a newtype of](https://docs.rs/struct.F8E5M2.html)

`F8E5M2`[by default. In binary formats this is ideal, as it will generally use just two bytes for storage. For string formats like JSON, however, this isn’t as useful, and due to design limitations of serde, it’s not possible for the default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html)

`u16``Serialize` implementation to support
different serialization for different formats.It is up to the container type of the floats to control how it is serialized. This can
easily be controlled when using the derive macros using `#[serde(serialize_with="")]`
attributes. For both [ F8E4M3](https://docs.rs/struct.F8E4M3.html) and

[, a](https://docs.rs/struct.F8E5M2.html)

`F8E5M2``serialize_as_f32` and `serialize_as_string` are
provided for use with this attribute.Deserialization of both float types supports deserializing from the default serialization,
strings, and `f32`/`f64` values, so no additional work is required.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

This crate supports a number of optional cargo features. None of these features are enabled by
default, even `std`.

-
`std``std`
-
`serde``serde``Serialize``Deserialize``F8E4M3``F8E5M2`
-
`num-traits``num-traits``ToPrimitive``FromPrimitive``AsPrimitive``Num``Float``FloatCore``Bounded``F8E4M3``F8E5M2`
-
`bytemuck``bytemuck``Zeroable``Pod``F8E4M3``F8E5M2`
-
`zerocopy``zerocopy``AsBytes``FromBytes``F8E4M3``F8E5M2`
-
`rand_distr``rand_distr``Distribution``F8E4M3``F8E5M2`
-
`rkyv``rkyv`

# half - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/half/^2.5.0/

## Expand description

A crate that provides support for half-precision 16-bit floating point types.

This crate provides the [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) type, which is an implementation of the IEEE 754-2008 standard

[a.k.a “half” floating point type. This 16-bit floating point type is intended for efficient storage where the full range and precision of a larger floating point value is not required. This is especially useful for image storage formats.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-precision_floating-point_format)

`binary16`This crate also provides a [ bf16](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html) type, an alternative 16-bit floating point format. The

[format is a truncated IEEE 754 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bfloat16_floating-point_format)

`bfloat16``binary32` float that preserves the
exponent to allow the same range as [but with only 8 bits of precision (instead of 11 bits for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`[). See the](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[type for details.](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`Because [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[are primarily for efficient storage, floating point operations such as addition, multiplication, etc. are not always implemented by hardware. When hardware does not support these operations, this crate emulates them by converting the value to](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[before performing the operation and then back afterward.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`Note that conversion from [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)/

[to both](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[are lossy operations, and just as converting a](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64`[is lossy and does not have](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32``Into`/`From` trait
implementations, so too do these smaller types not have those trait implementations either.
Instead, use `from_f32`/`from_f64` functions for the types in this crate. If you don’t care
about lossy conversions and need trait conversions, use the appropriate [traits that are implemented.](https://crates.io/crates/num-traits)

`num-traits`This crate also provides a [ slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html) module for zero-copy in-place conversions of

[slices to both](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html)

`u16`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[, as well as efficient vectorized conversions of larger buffers of floating point values to and from these half formats.](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`The crate supports `#[no_std]` when the `std` cargo feature is not enabled, so can be used in
embedded environments without using the Rust [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/) library. The

`std` feature enables support
for the standard library and is enabled by default, see the [Cargo Features](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)section below.

A [ prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html) module is provided for easy importing of available utility traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

When the `serde` feature is enabled, [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[will be serialized as a newtype of](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[by default. In binary formats this is ideal, as it will generally use just two bytes for storage. For string formats like JSON, however, this isn’t as useful, and due to design limitations of serde, it’s not possible for the default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html)

`u16``Serialize` implementation to support
different serialization for different formats.Instead, it’s up to the containter type of the floats to control how it is serialized. This can
easily be controlled when using the derive macros using `#[serde(serialize_with="")]`
attributes. For both [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[a](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16``serialize_as_f32` and `serialize_as_string` are
provided for use with this attribute.Deserialization of both float types supports deserializing from the default serialization,
strings, and `f32`/`f64` values, so no additional work is required.

[§](https://docs.rs#hardware-support)Hardware support

Hardware support for these conversions and arithmetic will be used
whenever hardware support is available—either through instrinsics or targeted assembly—although
a nightly Rust toolchain may be required for some hardware. When hardware supports it the
functions and traits in the [ slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html) and

[modules will also use vectorized SIMD intructions for increased efficiency.](https://docs.rs/vec/index.html)

`vec`The following list details hardware support for floating point types in this crate. When using
`std` cargo feature, runtime CPU target detection will be used. To get the most performance
benefits, compile for specific CPU features which avoids the runtime overhead and works in a
`no_std` environment.

| Architecture | CPU Target Feature | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x86`/`x86_64` | `f16c` | This supports conversion to/from only (including vector SIMD) and does not support any`f16`or arithmetic operations.`bf16` |
| `aarch64` | `fp16` | This supports all operations on only.`f16` |
| `loongarch64` | `lsx` | This supports conversion to/from only (including vector SIMD) and does not support any`f16`or arithmetic operations.`bf16` |

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

# rocm-rs: Safe Rust wrappers for AMD ROCm Libraries

This project provides Rust bindings for AMD's ROCm (Radeon Open Compute) libraries, allowing Rust developers to leverage AMD GPUs for high-performance computing.

## Disclaimer

This project is **not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)**.

ROCm and AMD are trademarks of Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.

## Current Status

**Note: This project is in early development.**

Currently implemented:

- ✅ rocFFT - Fast Fourier Transform library (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ HIP - Heterogeneous-Compute Interface for Portability (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ rocBLAS - Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ MIOpen - Deep learning primitives (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ rocRAND - Random number generation (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ rocSOLVER - Linear system solvers (raw bindings + safe wrappers)
- ✅ rocSPARSE - Sparse linear algebra (raw bindings only)
- ✅ ROCArray - GPU array struct with api similar to Vec (to be deprecated in favor of DeviceMemoryExt)
- ✅ rocmsmi - system managment interface (refer to [rocm_smi_lib](https://github.com/PTFOPlayer/rocm_smi_lib_rs))
- ✅ rocm_kernel_macros - macros for writing gpu kernels in rust(refer to [rocm_kernel_macros](https://github.com/RustNSparks/rocm_kernel_macros))

The project currently focuses on providing raw FFI bindings for most libraries, with safe Rust wrappers available for rocFFT. Additional safe wrappers for other libraries are planned for future development.

## Prerequisites

- AMD ROCm installed (version 6.3 or later recommended.It may work on older versions, but I did not test that)
- Ubuntu 24.04 / Fedora 42
- Rust toolchain (1.65.0 or later recommended)
- A compatible AMD GPU

## Installation

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "5.1"
```
## Usage

First, ensure that the ROCm libraries are in your library path or set the `ROCM_PATH` environment variable.

### Writing your own kernels with rust

```
use PathBuf;
use ;
const LEN: usize = 1024;
// initializing rust gpu kernel
amdgpu_kernel_init!;
// marking code that will be coppied to gpu kernel
// compiling gpu kernel
const AMDGPU_KERNEL_BINARY_PATH: &str = amdgpu_kernel_finalize!;
```
For async operations with streams:

```
use PathBuf;
use ;
const LEN: usize = 1024;
amdgpu_kernel_init!;
const AMDGPU_KERNEL_BINARY_PATH: &str = amdgpu_kernel_finalize!;
```
```
### Using rocFFT with safe wrappers:
```rust
use rocm_rs::rocfft::{self, plan, execution, field};
fn main() {
    // Initialize the rocFFT library
    // Use the safe wrappers for rocFFT
    let plan = plan::Plan::new(/* parameters */);
    let field = field::Field::new(/* parameters */);
    let execution = execution::Execution::new(/* parameters */);

    // Perform FFT operations
    // ...
}
```
### Using other libraries with raw bindings:

```
use *;
```
## Building from Source

**Important**: When building from source, you need to run `cargo build` first to generate the bindings files before you can use the library or run tests.

```
# Clone the repository
# Set the ROCm path if not in the default location
# Build the project (generates bindings)
```
## Feature flags

- rocm_smi - enables bindings and wrappers for rocm_smi_lib

## Examples

The project includes a workspace with examples for each sub-library. Run examples with:

### HIP

- `vector_add_example`- Vector addition with kernel written in HIP
- `rust_kernel`- Kernel written in Rust using macros
- `rust_kernel_async`- Async kernel execution with streams
- `saxpy`- SAXPY operation (Single-precision A*X + Y)
- `sort`- GPU sorting example

### MIOpen

- `miopen_basic`- Basic MIOpen usage example
- `multi_tensor`- Multi-tensor operations

### rocBLAS

- `rocblas_basic`- Basic rocBLAS usage example

### rocRAND

- `normal`- Random number generation with normal distribution

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome! Please feel free to submit a Pull Request.

When contributing:

- Run `cargo build`first to generate the bindings
- Add tests for new functionality
- Update documentation as needed

## License

This project is licensed under the MIT License - see the LICENSE file for details.

## Acknowledgments

- AMD for developing and maintaining ROCm
- The Rust community for bindgen and other tools used in this project
